title: IMF chief says AI risks may exceed opportunities without safeguards and ethical framework
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on October 16 that artificial intelligence’s risks could outweigh its opportunities unless safeguards and an ethical framework keep pace with development.

Speaking at the IMF–World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva supported a combination of industry self-regulation and government involvement. She said access to electricity, digital infrastructure and adequate regulation would help determine whether AI’s benefits reach people broadly, Reuters reported.

Her warning acknowledged AI’s contribution to economic growth while highlighting the possibility of negative shocks if productivity improvements arrive more slowly than expected. Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, participating in the discussion, backed standards and argued that oversight should extend beyond voluntary commitments.

Why it matters

The economic stakes extend beyond whether individual AI products perform well. The IMF identifies risks involving employment, unequal access, financial stability, cybersecurity and the concentration of technological power. It calls for stronger safeguards alongside investment in skills and digital infrastructure.

For businesses, that makes governance part of implementation. A practical response would include testing systems before deployment, assigning responsibility for consequential decisions and measuring whether promised efficiency gains actually appear. These are implications of the warning, rather than a detailed compliance framework announced at the meeting.

For workers, the issue is how quickly skills and support systems adapt as tasks change. For developing economies, unreliable electricity and limited connectivity could restrict participation even as wealthier countries accelerate adoption. The IMF highlights infrastructure, skills and social protection as essential policy priorities.

The central implication is that technical progress alone cannot guarantee shared prosperity. Safeguards must make AI dependable enough for widespread use, while public investment helps more people benefit. Georgieva’s warning places responsibility on both companies building the technology and governments managing its economic consequences. The challenge is turning that responsibility into practical, enforceable arrangements as capabilities advance.
